title: Summer Camp vs. Privates: What Actually Moves the Needle
description: Every June, gyms pitch one and parents buy the other. Here's what camp actually develops, what a private lesson can and can't fix, what each typically costs, and how to build a summer plan that shows up in October.
ogDescription: Camps build culture and composure. Privates build one named skill — but only with a specific problem to solve and a coach who can solve it. Here's how to decide.
headline: Summer camp vs. privates: what actually *moves the needle* — and what doesn't.
sub: Every June, gyms pitch one and parents sign up for the other. Neither side agrees on which is worth the money. Here's the honest breakdown — what each one develops, what each typically costs, and when the right answer is neither.

blocks.text: Every spring, once the season's results are posted and the group chat finally goes quiet for a week, the same question surfaces in every gym lobby in the country: *camp, privates, or both?* It arrives dressed as a scheduling question. It is actually a money question, a burnout question, and — most of the time — a question about which skill is standing between an athlete and the team she wants next season.

The short version, before the details: **camp builds composure and culture. Privates build one specific skill.** Spend on the wrong one for where your athlete currently is and you have not only wasted money — you may have spent the one recovery window in the calendar reinforcing a habit that will need to be un-taught in August.
The question underneath the question
Before comparing options, name the goal out loud. Summer training generally serves one of four purposes, and they are not interchangeable:

items: **Acquire a named skill** — a standing tuck, a full, a specific stunt position. This is a privates problem.
**Maintain what already exists** — keep tumbling from decaying over a long break. This is an open-gym or tumbling-class problem, and it is the cheapest of the four to solve.
**Build performance nerve** — perform in front of strangers, on unfamiliar mats, on someone else's schedule. This is a camp problem.
**Recover** — from injury, from a long season, or from a kid who is quietly done. This is a rest problem, and no purchase fixes it.

blocks.text: Most families skip this step and buy whatever was marketed to them in May. Answer the goal question in one sentence and the rest mostly decides itself.
What camp actually does

A well-run summer camp — a branded national camp or a serious gym-run week — gives an athlete three things that are hard to buy any other way: high-volume repetition under time pressure, coaching from people who are not her regular staff, and repeated performance in a low-stakes environment. That third one is chronically underrated.

Competition nerves are, in large part, a function of how rarely kids perform in front of strangers. An athlete who has performed several times a day for four days, in front of rotating evaluators and other teams, is a fundamentally different competitor in October than one who has only ever stunted inside her home gym with the same twenty faces watching. The routine may be identical. The nervous system is not.

Camp also does something quieter than skills work: it shapes what kind of teammate a kid becomes. Early call times, and the moment a stunt group fails in front of another gym and has to reset without sulking — that is where team culture gets built, and no amount of one-on-one coaching produces it.

**Camp tends to pay off for:** athletes in the lower and middle levels, new flyers and bases learning to trust each other, kids who freeze under performance pressure, athletes moving up a level who need mat volume before the season, and any team with significant roster turnover that needs to become a team before choreography lands.

**Camp will not fix:** a specific mechanical skill gap. Doing a flawed standing tuck forty more times at speed does not correct it; it laminates it. Camp also will not help an athlete who is injured, exhausted, or heading into her fifth consecutive summer of a curriculum she has memorized.
What a private lesson actually does

A private with a good coach is surgical. It identifies one mechanical problem — hip position at the peak of a tuck, hand placement on a lib, the timing of a dip on a basket — and gives the athlete a correction she can *feel*, plus something concrete to rehearse without the coach present. For the right problem, a single well-run session can accomplish what months of group practice cannot, because in group practice nobody is watching one set of hips for forty minutes.
"One good private is worth ten mediocre ones. The coach matters far more than the format."

The problem is that most privates sold in June are not surgical. Private lessons are among the **highest-margin products most gyms sell** — the equipment is already there, the space is already leased, and the session prices at a premium per hour. That is not a scandal; it is simply the economics, and it means the incentive to recommend privates broadly exists whether or not your particular athlete needs them.

A coach who runs your athlete through the same drills she already does in class, with slightly more attention, is not giving you a private lesson. She is giving you a tutoring session for a class that already isn't working — at four to six times the hourly rate.

**Privates earn the money when:** there is a specific, named skill on the table. The coach can articulate a progression and what the athlete should be able to do by session three. Progress is visible week to week. Your athlete is at a level where group practice genuinely cannot supply enough individual attention, or she is one skill away from a roster spot that materially changes her season.

**Privates do not earn the money when:** the gym recommends them to every family without a rationale specific to your kid. The coach changes each week, so nobody owns the progression. The athlete has not mastered the prerequisites for the skill being trained — which is the most common and most expensive version of this mistake. Or you are buying them because other families on the team are, which is the second most common.
The third option nobody pitches

There is no marketing budget behind rest, so nobody sends an email about it in May. But competitive cheer is a year-round, high-impact sport played largely by growing bodies, and the summer is the only real gap in the calendar. An athlete who trains through every week of it arrives at tryouts with no reserve.

Rest does not have to mean the couch. A few weeks of something else — swimming, a different sport, strength and mobility work, or simply a schedule with no drive to the gym in it — protects the thing you are actually paying for, which is a kid who still wants to do this in three years. Cross-training in particular tends to return more than another tumbling hour for athletes who have plateaued: ankles, hips and shoulders that are stronger and better balanced make the skill work possible in the fall.

If your athlete is carrying a nagging injury — wrist, back, ankle, shoulder — summer is when it gets addressed, not deferred. A season built on top of an unresolved injury tends to end early, and the cost of that ending is not measured in dollars.
What each option typically costs

Pricing varies widely by region, gym size and coach seniority, so treat everything below as planning ranges rather than quotes. The useful comparison is not which line is cheapest — it is what each line actually buys.

blocks.text: Notice that the two cheapest rows solve two of the four goals listed at the top. Maintenance and recovery are common needs and cheap to meet; acquisition and performance nerve are the expensive ones. Families get into trouble paying acquisition prices for a maintenance problem.
How to tell a real private from a revenue line
You do not need to be a technical expert to evaluate a private lesson. You need four questions, asked before you book the block rather than after it:

items: **What specific skill are we working on, and what's the current obstacle?** A good coach names both without hesitating. "Just general tumbling" is not an answer worth $120 an hour.
**What should she be able to do by the end of the third session?** This is the single most clarifying question in the sport. Coaches who work from a progression have an answer.
**What is she practicing on her own between sessions?** If nothing, the session is not transferring, and you are renting attention rather than buying development.
**Is it the same coach every week?** Consistency is most of the value. A rotating cast restarts the diagnosis every session, on your dime.

blocks.text: One more test, applied at the end: if you cannot describe what changed after a block of privates — in plain language, not vibes — the block did not work, and repeating it in the fall will not work either.
Building the summer plan by level
Lower levels and first-year athletes

Camp, or a gym-run week, plus open gym. At this stage the limiting factors are confidence, body awareness and simply being comfortable on a floor. Volume and fun beat precision. Privates are usually premature unless there is one skill blocking a level move, and even then a short block beats a standing weekly commitment.
Middle levels

This is where the real judgment call lives. Most middle-level athletes are served best by camp plus a small, targeted block of privates for one named skill — not a summer-long standing appointment. If the season ended with a skill that was almost there, this is the moment it gets finished. If nothing specific is missing, camp and maintenance are enough.
Upper levels

Individual attention starts to matter more than group volume, because the skills are specific enough that group practice cannot service them. Privates with a consistent coach, plus strength work, plus enough rest to arrive at tryouts healthy. Camp still has value for a team with heavy turnover, but at this level the athlete typically brings composure with her already.
The recommendation

If you are choosing one thing: **camp for the lower and middle levels, targeted privates for the upper levels** — with the standing caveat that privates only work when there is a named skill to fix and a consistent coach who can fix it.

If you are being pressured toward both, ask the gym to name the specific skill that makes weekly privates necessary *for your athlete, right now*. A good coach will answer immediately and specifically. If the answer is general — "she'd benefit," "everyone on that team does them" — then the honest recommendation was camp, maintenance, or rest, and the invoice was just easier to write the other way.

And if the summer budget simply is not there this year, that is survivable. Open gym, a stretching routine at home, and an athlete who arrives in August rested and still in love with the sport is a respectable summer. Plenty of athletes have had exactly that one and made the team.
The gyms that sell the most summer training are not always the ones fielding the best athletes in October. Keep that distinction in mind before you write the check.
